content: Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS), also referred to as neonatal aspiration of meconium, occurs when an infant inhales meconium into their lungs either during or before delivery. Meconium is the first stool of a newborn, consisting of materials ingested while in the uterus, such as intestinal epithelial cells, lanugo (fine fetal hair), mucus, amniotic fluid, bile, and water. Unlike later feces, meconium is sterile and odorless. Normally, meconium is stored in the infant's intestines until after birth. However, in some cases, often due to fetal distress, it is expelled into the amniotic fluid before or during labor. If the baby inhales this contaminated fluid, respiratory complications may arise. Meconium passage into the amniotic fluid occurs in approximately 5–20% of all births, with a higher prevalence in post-term deliveries. However, MAS develops in only 5–10% of these cases. Fetal distress during labor frequently triggers intestinal contractions and relaxation of the anal sphincter, allowing meconium to mix with the amniotic fluid. Normally clear, amniotic fluid becomes greenish when stained with meconium. If the infant inhales this mixture before, during, or after birth, it can be drawn deep into the lungs. This can lead to three primary issues: airway obstruction by the material, reduced efficiency of gas exchange in the lungs, and irritation or inflammation of the airways, potentially resulting in chemical pneumonia. Approximately one-third of infants with MAS require respiratory support. The most apparent sign of meconium aspiration is the greenish discoloration of the amniotic fluid. If meconium was passed long before delivery, the infant's skin may also appear green-stained. Other signs include rapid or labored breathing, a slow heart rate, or a low Apgar score. Diagnosis of inhalation can be confirmed through various methods, such as listening for abnormal lung sounds with a stethoscope, performing blood gas tests, or using chest X-rays to identify patchy or streaked areas in the lungs. Infants who have inhaled meconium often develop respiratory distress, which may necessitate ventilatory support. Complications of MAS include pneumothorax (collapsed lung) and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Imaging findings in MAS may reveal high lung volumes due to small airway obstruction, asymmetric and patchy pulmonary opacities, pleural effusions, and pneumothorax in 20–40% of cases, also secondary to small airway obstruction. Preventing MAS is challenging. However, ensuring delivery before 42 weeks of gestation may reduce the risk. Amnioinfusion, a procedure in which sterile fluid is introduced into the uterus via a catheter to dilute thick meconium in the amniotic fluid, has been used as a preventive measure. However, recent studies have not demonstrated significant benefits from this approach. Previously, it was recommended that the obstetrician suction the baby’s throat and nose immediately after the head is delivered, but newer studies have shown this to be ineffective. Consequently, the revised Neonatal Resuscitation Guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics no longer recommend routine suctioning. If meconium-stained amniotic fluid is present and the baby is born in a depressed state, it is advised that a pediatrician suction the mouth and nose and use a laryngoscope and suction catheter to remove meconium from below the vocal cords. In severe cases where standard treatments fail to improve the newborn's condition, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) may be employed as a last resort.
